content:
Earlier this year, I swapped a battery-powered push mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. Users need to manually drive it around the perimeter of the yard to build a virtual map. Once set up, the machine will automatically perform mowing tasks according to a predetermined schedule.

Recently, I tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I believe it may be an easier choice for many people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year is how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I needed to manually drive the mower along the perimeter with my iPhone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. Three cameras allow the mower to automatically map the lawn, without the need to pre-install boundary wires or an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic method takes longer to create the initial map. However, I think for people who are not particularly tech-savvy, this approach may be easier to get started with.

To verify this claim, I specifically asked my mum, who lives in another state, to install and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She replied that everything worked fine. But I'm not entirely sure she would have the patience to first manually drive the robot around the entire perimeter, and then manually mark the areas to avoid.

The automatic mapping threw up a small quirk in my front yard. There is no fence or other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbour's, so TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's grass in my map.

I then resolved the issue by marking that section as a no-go zone in the app. However, if a lawn has no clear visual boundary, extra care may be needed during the initial mapping process.

Seeing through the mower's cameras

TerraMow's cameras also support one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show in real time what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to open that view in a large window. That way I could work indoors while watching the mower navigate the backyard from its own perspective.

This feature is not essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting and can sometimes help explain why it slows down or avoids certain things. The Anthbot M9 does not offer a similar camera view.

The two iPhone apps share a lot of similar design elements in other respects. Both allow scheduling jobs, adjusting mowing behaviour, dividing zones, marking areas to avoid, and remote-controlling the mower.

On that last feature, TerraMow has a particularly nice variation. In addition to the traditional left/right virtual controls, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and guide the mower with your thumb.

Manually controlling the mower with an iPhone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should operate on its own according to a predetermined schedule without any intervention. However, TerraMow's joystick control is surprisingly useful for cleaning up missed spots.

Sometimes, I feel almost as if I'm controlling the robot with telekinesis (that pleasant kind of feeling). I can hold the iPhone down at my side and walk, and with just a slight movement of my thumb, the machine will travel in my direction.

All robotic mower apps should copy this control method.

A more aggressive mower

Overall, the TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was also noisier while working.

I wouldn't call TerraMow loud. But the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot can run so quietly that it's easy to forget it's still going, including when it mows after sunset using its headlight.

Since TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. That makes daytime scheduling more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and sturdy, and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage with the machine that can cover the charging dock, whereas Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been stable and reliable. I've relied on it to handle the mowing for several weeks straight without needing to step in myself.

When adaptive maps get too clever

The visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continually updates its map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these updates takes some time, during which you temporarily can't do anything else in the app.

After several consecutive days of rain, I ran into an interesting edge case. Puddles formed in parts of the yard, and TerraMow reasonably avoided that area during its next run.

The grass within the skipped circular area then started to grow taller. Over time, the mower seemed to treat that patch of tall grass as something it should continue to avoid, and even after the ground had dried, that patch of grass was still consistently left out.

I used the remote control function in the app to manually drive over that patch of tall grass to trim it, which resolved the issue. Once that area looked like normal lawn again, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regular edging also helps TerraMow reach the boundary with more confidence. If the grass along an indistinct boundary grows too tall, it may be treated as an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive and more reliant on boundaries and obstacles set by the user. That method requires more upfront work, but at the same time it avoids the map "changing its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac's take

Having used both systems, for most people I lean towards TerraMow's camera-based approach.

Pre-installing boundary wires is a complete non-starter for me, and installing an RTK base station adds another piece of hardware that needs to be positioned, powered and maintained. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. The initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property line needed manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook tall grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 delivers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, a compelling live camera view, and the best manual control experience I've come across in a robotic mower app.

I genuinely enjoy working in the yard, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. Handing that task over to a robot gives me more time to tend to landscaping, edging and detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 does this well enough that I would recommend it, especially for anyone who wants robotic mowing but doesn't want to bury wires, install an RTK antenna, or manually walk an iPhone around the entire yard.

Amazon currently lists the TerraMow V1000 at $999 after applying a $200 coupon on the site. You can also find this product on TerraMow's official website.
